title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 outage from accidental removal of billing subsystem servers
rawText:
Impact
Amazon S3 in the US-EAST-1 region was unavailable for approximately 3 hours and 13 minutes on February 28 2017. The S3 console, the S3 PUT and DELETE APIs, and S3's ability to retrieve object metadata were all severely impacted. A large number of websites and services that depend on S3 experienced elevated error rates or complete unavailability. AWS's own services that rely on S3 for metadata storage, including EC2, EBS, Lambda, and the AWS Management Console, were also degraded. Hundreds of well-known websites and SaaS products were partially or fully unavailable during the incident.

Timeline
09:37 PST - Engineer begins executing a command to remove a small number of servers from the S3 billing subsystem.
09:37 PST - Due to a parameter input error, a significantly larger set of index servers is removed than intended.
09:39 PST - S3 API begins returning errors as the index tier loses quorum.
09:45 PST - AWS begins receiving alerts from monitoring systems. Incident declared.
10:00 PST - Engineers identify the root cause. Begin planning restart sequence.
10:27 PST - Restart of index tier begins. S3 API remains unavailable during restart.
12:26 PST - Full S3 index server restart completes across all capacity. S3 service restored.
12:50 PST - All S3 APIs return to full normal operation.

Root Cause
An engineer executing a routine capacity reduction exercise on the S3 billing subsystem ran a command that was intended to remove a small number of servers but entered an incorrect input parameter. This caused a much larger set of index servers to be removed than intended. Removing the index servers meant the S3 metadata index tier lost quorum and could no longer serve read or write requests. The S3 control plane requires the index tier to be operational to process any API calls. The operational tool that executed the removal did not have a built-in safety limit on what percentage of a cluster's capacity could be removed in a single operation. The restart of index servers was itself time-consuming because S3 had not restarted the index tier at full scale in some years and many of the safeguards and processes had not been exercised at this scale.

Fix
AWS updated the tooling that modifies S3 subsystem capacity to require a minimum wait period before removing a large percentage of servers and to enforce a maximum percentage of capacity that can be removed in a single operation. Engineers practiced the full restart sequence of the index subsystem to establish baseline timing. S3 internal dashboards were improved to surface the health of subsystem components more clearly. The billing subsystem maintenance schedule was updated to allow more thorough review of commands before execution.

title: Slack global degradation from connection storm on first day back from holiday
rawText:
Impact
On January 4 2021, the first working day of the year, Slack experienced widespread degraded service affecting its ability to load and connect for millions of users. Customers were unable to connect to Slack at all, experienced disconnections, or saw significant delays in message delivery and channel loading. The degradation persisted for approximately 5 hours from 07:01 UTC to approximately 12:00 UTC. All Slack workspace types and tiers were affected including free, Pro, Business+, and Enterprise Grid.

Timeline
07:01 UTC - User connections begin spiking as business hours start globally on the first working day after a two-week holiday.
07:17 UTC - Automated alerts fire for elevated error rates on connection endpoints.
07:21 UTC - On-call engineer declares an incident. Initial hypothesis: upstream provider issue.
07:35 UTC - DNS resolution latency spike identified in Consul service discovery layer.
07:55 UTC - Engineers discover Consul agent cache has been exhausted by connection storm volume.
08:30 UTC - Mitigation attempts applied to connection tier. Partial recovery for some regions.
09:15 UTC - Load balancer configuration changes applied to spread connection reconnects over a longer window.
10:02 UTC - Service begins recovering. New connections succeeding at near-normal rates.
11:45 UTC - Full recovery confirmed across all regions. Incident closed.

Root Cause
Slack's backend uses Consul for service discovery. During normal operation, the Consul agent caches service endpoint lookups. On the first working day after the December holiday, millions of clients that had been idle for days all attempted to reconnect simultaneously within a narrow time window. This created a connection storm that overwhelmed the Consul DNS caching layer: because all clients were reconnecting from scratch, the Consul agent cache was cold and every connection required a fresh service discovery lookup. The volume of concurrent DNS resolution requests exceeded what Consul could serve within acceptable latency, causing resolution timeouts. Failed connections triggered immediate client retries, compounding the problem in a feedback loop. Load balancers were not configured with backoff or jitter on failed connection attempts, so retry storms were not dampened.

Fix
Slack implemented exponential backoff with jitter on client reconnection logic to prevent thundering-herd reconnect storms. Consul agent cache was pre-warmed for the set of services most frequently looked up at connection establishment. Connection tier capacity was increased in advance of known high-traffic dates (first day back from major holidays, launch days). Load balancer configuration was updated to enforce a connection rate limit per client to prevent individual clients from overwhelming the system with retries. DNS caching TTLs were tuned to reduce fresh-lookup volume during traffic spikes.

title: Redis OOM eviction causes cache stampede and database overload
rawText:
Impact
The account balance lookup service was unavailable for 1 hour 42 minutes on August 15 2022 from 14:07 UTC to 15:49 UTC. Customers were unable to view their account balance, make card payments, or complete transfers. Approximately 94,000 customer requests failed during the outage window. Payment card authorizations timed out after 30 seconds causing declined transactions at point-of-sale terminals.

Timeline
13:55 UTC - Redis memory utilization crosses 92%. Eviction policy (allkeys-lru) begins silently removing cached keys.
14:07 UTC - Balance lookup error rate spikes from 0.02% to 67% as cache hit rate drops from 95% to 3%.
14:09 UTC - Automated alert fires for balance-service error rate. On-call paged.
14:14 UTC - Engineer identifies Redis eviction in progress. Attempts to add Redis memory: blocked by capacity constraints in availability zone.
14:22 UTC - PostgreSQL database CPU spikes to 100% from cache miss traffic hitting the DB directly.
14:30 UTC - PostgreSQL connection pool exhausted. balance-service pods begin returning 503.
14:35 UTC - Engineers disable non-critical background jobs to reduce DB connection pressure.
14:55 UTC - Additional PostgreSQL read replica provisioned. Traffic shed to replica.
15:20 UTC - Redis memory freed by deleting stale session tokens (20GB recovered). Cache begins repopulating.
15:49 UTC - Cache hit rate restored above 90%. Error rate drops below 0.1%. Incident closed.

Root Cause
The Redis cluster was running at 78% memory utilization as a baseline, with an allkeys-lru eviction policy configured. A batch job processing end-of-month transaction reconciliation ran earlier than scheduled and loaded an unexpectedly large dataset into Redis (approximately 18GB of intermediate results). This pushed Redis memory utilization above the eviction threshold. The eviction policy silently removed the most recently least-used keys, which included the high-value balance cache entries. When balance-service cache hits dropped from 95% to near zero, every balance lookup fell through to the PostgreSQL database. The database had not been sized to handle the full uncached request volume. The combination of cache stampede and full DB load caused connection pool exhaustion, which caused the balance-service pods to fail outright rather than degrade gracefully.

Fix
Redis cluster memory was expanded from 32GB to 80GB with auto-scaling enabled at 60% utilization. The batch reconciliation job was moved to a separate Redis cluster isolated from the production cache. The eviction policy was changed to volatile-lru so only keys with explicit TTLs can be evicted, protecting permanent cache entries. A circuit breaker was added to balance-service that returns stale cached data if the database connection pool exceeds 80% utilization, rather than allowing requests to pile up. Redis memory utilization alerts were added at 70% and 85% thresholds. A cache warm-up procedure was documented and automated for use after any Redis restart.

title: Kubernetes pod OOMKill cascade from memory leak causes API service degradation
rawText:
Impact
Notion's core API service was degraded for 2 hours 17 minutes on March 22 2023. Page load times increased from 200ms median to over 8 seconds. Approximately 35% of API requests returned 504 Gateway Timeout errors. Real-time collaboration features (presence indicators and live cursors) were fully unavailable during the incident. The degradation affected all workspace types and regions.

Timeline
02:00 UTC - Deployment of collaboration-service v2.14.1 completes across all pods.
04:30 UTC - Memory consumption on collaboration-service pods begins gradual increase (baseline 280MB, trending to 340MB).
07:15 UTC - First collaboration-service pod hits 512MB memory limit. Kubernetes OOMKills the pod.
07:15 UTC - Pod restarts and begins accumulating memory again from scratch.
07:47 UTC - Three pods OOMKilled simultaneously. Kubernetes HPA detects high CPU from remaining pods and scales up. New pods start healthy but begin leaking immediately.
08:02 UTC - 11 of 16 collaboration-service pods OOMKilled within 15 minutes. Service degraded.
08:05 UTC - On-call paged on 504 error rate spike. Engineer identifies OOMKill cascade in kubectl.
08:19 UTC - Decision made to roll back to v2.14.0. Rollback initiated.
08:44 UTC - Rollback complete across all pods. Memory stabilizes. Error rate drops.
09:22 UTC - Full service recovery confirmed. Memory metrics normal.
09:35 UTC - Post-incident review begun. Memory profile comparison between v2.14.0 and v2.14.1 identifies WebSocket listener leak.

Root Cause
The v2.14.1 release of collaboration-service introduced a new WebSocket event listener registration in the presence tracking module. The listener was registered on connection establishment but not deregistered on connection close. Under normal load with connections cycling, each pod accumulated one listener per WebSocket connection lifetime. After approximately 5.5 hours at sustained load (~3,000 concurrent connections per pod), accumulated unregistered listeners consumed enough memory to exceed the 512MB pod memory limit. The Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scaled up new pods in response to the OOMKill cascade, but new pods immediately began leaking and hit the memory limit themselves within 90 minutes, preventing autoscaling from helping.

Fix
The WebSocket listener deregistration was added on connection close in v2.14.2. Memory limits on collaboration-service pods were increased temporarily from 512MB to 1GB to provide a safety margin. A memory growth rate alert was added: any pod with memory increasing at more than 5MB/hour triggers a Slack alert to the on-call engineer. The memory limit was also set as a soft limit alongside a hard limit to allow Kubernetes to kill the pod gracefully before it becomes a node-level issue. A 48-hour memory soak test was added to the staging environment CI pipeline for any changes to the collaboration-service. Rollback procedures were documented and practiced.

title: SSL certificate expiry causes webhook delivery failures and silent data loss
rawText:
Impact
PagerDuty webhook delivery to customer-configured endpoints failed silently for 4 hours 11 minutes on June 8 2021. Customers relying on webhooks for alert routing to Slack, Microsoft Teams, and custom integrations did not receive incident notifications. Approximately 18,400 webhooks were dropped without delivery confirmation. Some customers missed critical alert escalations during the window. The SSL certificate for the webhook delivery microservice had expired at 06:22 UTC and was not renewed until 10:33 UTC.

Timeline
06:22 UTC - SSL certificate for webhook-delivery.internal expires. No automated renewal triggers.
06:22 UTC - TLS handshake failures begin for all outbound webhook HTTPS connections.
06:23 UTC - webhook-delivery service logs TLS errors but retry logic continues retrying without alerting.
06:30 UTC - Scheduled certificate expiry check (runs hourly) fires alert, but alert goes to a legacy email alias no longer actively monitored.
06:35 UTC - First customer support ticket arrives reporting no Slack notifications for active incident.
08:47 UTC - Support escalates to on-call engineer after pattern of tickets identified.
08:52 UTC - Engineer identifies certificate expiry from webhook service logs.
09:10 UTC - Emergency certificate renewal process begun. Signing authority contacted.
10:33 UTC - New certificate deployed. TLS handshakes resume. Webhook delivery restores.
11:15 UTC - Backlog of 18,400 pending webhooks fully drained and delivered.

Root Cause
The webhook-delivery microservice used a manually provisioned TLS certificate with a 1-year expiry. The certificate renewal process was documented but required a manual step to deploy the renewed certificate. An automated check was configured to alert 30 days before expiry, but the alert destination was a team email alias that had been migrated to a new alias 8 months prior. The original alias still existed but was not actively monitored. The certificate expired without any engineer receiving an actionable alert. The webhook delivery retry logic continued attempting redelivery after TLS failures but did not distinguish TLS errors from transient network errors, so no separate alert was raised for the specific failure mode. Customer-facing dashboards did not surface webhook delivery health metrics, so customers had no visibility into the silent failures.

Fix
All TLS certificates were migrated to automated renewal via Let's Encrypt with a 60-day certificate rotation cycle. Certificate expiry monitoring was moved from email-alias alerts to PagerDuty itself with escalation to the infrastructure on-call. Webhook delivery health metrics (success rate, TLS error rate, queue depth) were added to a customer-facing status page dashboard. The webhook retry logic was updated to raise a distinct alert after 100 consecutive TLS failures to a single destination. All internal service email aliases were audited and deprecated aliases removed. A runbook for emergency certificate renewal was documented and added to the on-call playbook.

title: Stripe API latency degradation from payment service connection pool exhaustion
rawText:
Impact
Stripe's payment API experienced significant latency degradation from 04:12 UTC to 07:05 UTC on July 10 2019 lasting 2 hours 53 minutes. The p99 latency for payment charge creation increased from 340ms to over 15 seconds. Approximately 1.7% of all payment API calls during the window failed with timeout errors. Merchants relying on synchronous charge confirmation for e-commerce checkouts experienced elevated cart abandonment rates. The direct financial impact to merchants was estimated in the millions of dollars in failed transactions.

Timeline
04:12 UTC - p99 latency for payment charge creation begins climbing above 3-second SLO threshold.
04:18 UTC - Automated alert fires for payment API p99 threshold breach.
04:23 UTC - On-call engineer begins investigating. PostgreSQL connection pool metrics examined.
04:35 UTC - PostgreSQL primary identified as saturated: connection pool at 100% utilization.
04:42 UTC - Source identified: a new metadata write path added in a recent deploy is holding connections open 8x longer than expected.
05:00 UTC - Decision made to roll back the metadata path change. Rollback initiated.
05:14 UTC - Rollback complete. PostgreSQL connection pool utilization begins dropping.
05:45 UTC - p99 latency returns to below 500ms. Error rate drops below 0.1%.
07:05 UTC - Full normalization of all latency metrics. Incident closed.

Root Cause
A recent deploy added a new metadata field write to the payment charge creation path. The code that wrote this field opened a separate database connection for each charge request rather than reusing a connection from the pool. The new code path also held this connection open for the duration of an external HTTP call to a metadata enrichment service, which added an average of 800ms of hold time per connection. Under normal load the pool could absorb this. During a sustained traffic surge triggered by a major US e-commerce event, the combination of 8x longer per-connection hold time and elevated request volume caused the PostgreSQL connection pool to become fully saturated. Once the pool was saturated, new payment requests queued waiting for an available connection. Queue depth grew faster than connections were released, causing cascading latency increases.

Fix
The metadata write path was refactored to reuse connections from the shared pool and to not hold a connection open during external HTTP calls. A maximum connection hold-time limit was enforced in the database access layer with an alert when any code path held a connection for more than 200ms. Load testing of the payment charge path was added to the CI pipeline to detect connection pool pressure under simulated peak load. PostgreSQL connection pool dashboards were added to the on-call runbook. A circuit breaker was added to the metadata write path so that if the external metadata service is slow, the metadata write is deferred to an async queue rather than blocking the payment path.

title: BullMQ worker deadlock causes 6-hour job backlog and delayed email notifications
rawText:
Impact
Email notification delivery was delayed by 4 to 7 hours for all Render customers from 22:30 UTC September 11 to 04:45 UTC September 12 2023. Build completion notifications, deployment success and failure alerts, and billing notifications were all affected. Approximately 340,000 email jobs accumulated in the queue. The delay affected all Render workspace tiers.

Timeline
18:00 UTC - Scheduled deployment of notification-worker v3.8.0 with new retry logic.
18:15 UTC - Deployment completes. Worker pods appear healthy in Kubernetes.
22:30 UTC - Email job throughput drops from 800 jobs/minute to 0. Queue depth begins growing.
22:48 UTC - Email delivery lag alert fires. On-call paged.
22:55 UTC - Engineer checks notification-worker pods: all appear Running with 0 restarts.
23:10 UTC - Worker logs show jobs being picked up (status: active) but never completing.
23:20 UTC - BullMQ job stall detection identifies 4,000 jobs stuck in active state for >5 minutes.
23:35 UTC - Engineer identifies that worker process is blocked inside the new retry logic waiting on a Redis MULTI/EXEC transaction that never completes.
00:02 UTC - Decision to rollback to v3.7.2. New worker pods deployed.
00:14 UTC - Rollback complete. Stuck jobs drain and re-enter queue. Processing resumes.
04:45 UTC - Job backlog fully cleared. Email delivery lag returns to <2 minutes.

Root Cause
The v3.8.0 release added a new retry-with-backoff mechanism to the notification-worker. The retry logic used a Redis MULTI/EXEC transaction to atomically check a rate limit counter and update a retry timestamp. The MULTI/EXEC block contained a WATCH command on the rate limit key. Under concurrent worker execution, WATCH-triggered transaction aborts (EXECABORT) were not handled: the code waited indefinitely for the transaction to complete. Each worker goroutine that encountered an EXECABORT locked the job in active state and blocked, waiting for a transaction response that would never arrive. Because BullMQ marks jobs as active when a worker picks them up, all 4,000 jobs that were picked up during the deadlock window were locked in active state until the stall timeout (set to 30 seconds) eventually moved them to failed state, but the dead workers continued holding locks.

Fix
The MULTI/EXEC WATCH pattern was replaced with a Lua script executed atomically on the Redis server, eliminating the possibility of EXECABORT. BullMQ worker stall detection timeout was reduced from 30 seconds to 5 seconds. An alert was added for any worker where job active time exceeds 3x the expected processing time. A load test was added to the notification-worker CI pipeline that simulates concurrent workers processing 10,000 jobs to catch deadlock scenarios before deployment. Worker rollback runbook was documented with step-by-step instructions.

title: Logging server disk exhaustion causes silent write failures and data corruption
rawText:
Impact
Honeycomb's ingest pipeline dropped approximately 14% of all trace spans submitted between 01:15 UTC and 06:43 UTC on November 3 2022. Customers experienced gaps in their observability data: queries against traces ingested during the window showed incomplete results. High-volume enterprise customers with SLA-backed trace retention had complete data loss for 5-hour windows. The silent nature of the failure meant no customer-visible error was raised; traces appeared to be accepted but were not durably stored.

Timeline
23:00 UTC Nov 2 - Weekly log rotation job fails silently. Old log files not compressed and rotated.
01:15 UTC Nov 3 - /var/log partition on ingest-primary-01 reaches 100% capacity.
01:15 UTC Nov 3 - Write-ahead log (WAL) for the ingest buffer cannot write new entries. Buffer accepts incoming spans into memory but cannot flush to disk.
01:30 UTC Nov 3 - Memory buffer on ingest-primary-01 fills. Spans begin being silently dropped.
02:40 UTC Nov 3 - Disk usage alert configured at 95% threshold does not fire because alert targets /data partition, not /var/log.
03:15 UTC Nov 3 - Customer support ticket: traces missing for 2-hour window. Triaged as potential query bug.
05:45 UTC Nov 3 - Second customer ticket. Engineer escalates to ingest team.
05:52 UTC Nov 3 - Engineer identifies disk-full on /var/log partition from system metrics.
05:58 UTC Nov 3 - Failed log rotation identified. Old log files manually compressed. Disk freed.
06:43 UTC Nov 3 - WAL resumes. Ingest pipeline back to full operation.

Root Cause
The weekly log rotation cron job relied on logrotate with a copytruncate option. A temporary file permission change made during a security audit changed the ownership of /var/log/ingest to a non-root user. logrotate ran as root and could not write the compressed output files to the directory. The job exited with an error but was not configured to send alerts on failure, so the failure went undetected for a week. Over the following 7 days, unrotated log files accumulated until the partition was full. The disk alert was configured against the /data partition (where trace data is stored) but not against /var/log. The ingest buffer's write-ahead log silently dropped spans once it could not flush to disk rather than returning an error to the HTTP ingest endpoint, meaning clients received 200 OK responses for spans that were never durably stored.

Fix
Log rotation job was migrated to a systemd timer with explicit alerting on failure. Disk usage monitoring was expanded to all partitions above 50GB, not just the data partition. Alerts were set at 80% and 90% capacity for all monitored partitions. The ingest buffer was updated to return HTTP 503 to clients when it cannot flush the WAL to disk, so clients can implement retry logic. A monthly disk capacity review was added to the infrastructure on-call runbook. File permission changes now trigger an automated check of all cron jobs and scheduled tasks that require write access to affected directories.

title: Fastly CDN misconfiguration caches 500 error pages causing users to see stale errors
rawText:
Impact
Vercel users deploying new projects experienced 500 error pages that persisted for up to 55 minutes after the underlying issue was resolved on May 17 2023. The CDN cache was serving stale 500 error responses for approximately 2 hours from 09:33 UTC to 11:41 UTC. Approximately 12,000 unique domains served cached 500 error pages to end users. Customers who had successfully deployed working code saw their users receive error pages because the CDN continued serving the cached error response even after the origin returned 200 responses.

Timeline
08:45 UTC - A configuration deployment changes Fastly VCL for the edge project serving layer.
09:33 UTC - A transient database connectivity issue causes the origin to return 500 errors for 4 minutes on project page requests.
09:37 UTC - Origin recovers. Database connectivity restored. Origin returns 200 for all requests.
09:38 UTC - Engineers notice 500 error rate spike and begin investigating.
09:45 UTC - Origin confirmed healthy. Engineers assume incident resolved.
10:12 UTC - Customer tickets begin arriving: still seeing 500 errors despite origin being healthy.
10:20 UTC - Engineer realizes CDN is still serving cached 500 responses.
10:25 UTC - Root cause identified: the VCL configuration change set cache TTL for all 5xx responses to 3600 seconds.
10:31 UTC - Fastly cache purge for all affected domains initiated.
11:41 UTC - Cache fully purged across all Fastly PoPs globally. 200 responses serving from origin confirmed.

Root Cause
A VCL (Varnish Configuration Language) configuration update was deployed to the Fastly edge layer. The change was intended to improve cache hit rate for static assets by increasing their TTL. However, the VCL template had a logic error: the TTL override applied to all responses including error responses, not just successful responses. The change set `set beresp.ttl = 3600s;` unconditionally, meaning 500 error responses received a 1-hour TTL. When the transient origin error occurred 48 minutes after the VCL deployment, Fastly cached those 500 responses with a 1-hour TTL. Even after the origin recovered, Fastly continued serving the cached error pages to all users. The VCL change was not reviewed for error-response side effects and the staging environment for VCL changes did not simulate origin error conditions.

Fix
The VCL template was updated to explicitly set TTL to 0 for all 4xx and 5xx responses, using an if-else block rather than an unconditional assignment. VCL configuration changes were added to a mandatory security and correctness review checklist. Automated tests were added to the VCL deployment pipeline that simulate origin 4xx and 5xx responses and assert that error responses are never cached by the CDN. Fastly cache purge procedures were documented and added to the on-call runbook as a first step when users report errors after origin recovery. Real-time CDN cache hit/miss dashboards for error responses were added to the incident command dashboard.

title: GitHub 24-hour degradation from MySQL master failover during datacenter maintenance
rawText:
Impact
GitHub.com experienced 24 hours and 11 minutes of service degradation beginning October 21 2018 at 22:52 UTC. During this period, many features were either unavailable or operating in a degraded mode: push events, pull request creation, repository creation, and the issue tracker were all affected for periods of the outage. Notifications, stars, and watch counts were temporarily inconsistent. GitHub's blob storage (used for file serving and LFS) was completely unavailable for approximately 3 hours. Total affected user time across all regions was significant.

Timeline
22:52 UTC Oct 21 - Scheduled network maintenance begins in primary US-EAST datacenter. 43-second network partition occurs.
22:52 UTC Oct 21 - MySQL Orchestrator detects loss of primary and automatically promotes a replica in the US-WEST datacenter to primary.
22:53 UTC Oct 21 - Original US-EAST primary comes back online. Two MySQL primaries now exist: US-EAST (original) and US-WEST (promoted).
22:55 UTC Oct 21 - Application traffic splits: some pods still connect to US-EAST primary, others connect to US-WEST promoted primary. Writes are accepted by both.
23:07 UTC Oct 21 - Engineers notified of replication anomaly. Incident declared.
23:15 UTC Oct 21 - Decision made to failover entirely to US-WEST promoted primary. Original US-EAST primary taken offline.
00:30 UTC Oct 22 - With single primary established, GitHub begins verifying data consistency. Inconsistencies found.
03:00 UTC Oct 22 - GitHub staff begin manual reconciliation of inconsistent data using event log replay.
10:15 UTC Oct 22 - Blob storage fully restored. Core services begin recovering.
23:03 UTC Oct 22 - All features confirmed fully restored. Incident closed.

Root Cause
GitHub uses a MySQL topology managed by Orchestrator, an open-source tool for automatic MySQL failover. During a 43-second network partition caused by scheduled maintenance, Orchestrator detected the loss of the primary and promoted a US-WEST replica to primary as designed. When the network partition ended and the original US-EAST primary came back online, both Orchestrator and some application pods briefly treated it as the authoritative primary. During the approximately 2-minute window of dual-primary operation, writes were accepted by both servers. The resulting divergence in write-ahead logs caused data inconsistencies that persisted after the cluster was reunified under a single primary. GitHub's application layer did not have a mechanism to detect or reject writes during the split-brain window.

Fix
Orchestrator was configured with a mandatory hold-off period before promoting a replica when a primary is lost: the promotion is delayed 5 minutes to allow transient network partitions to resolve before declaring the primary dead. Application pods were updated to include a primary-identity check that rejects writes when it cannot confirm the identity of the database primary from Orchestrator's topology API. A data consistency checker was built that continuously compares row counts and checksums across replicas and raises an alert on any divergence. GitHub's internal incident response playbook was updated to include split-brain scenarios with clear decision criteria for when to take an old primary offline. The Orchestrator configuration was open-sourced as a best-practices reference for MySQL failover configuration.
